When exactly Kuang Anshi became capable of standing on his own, even he himself couldn't say for certain.
Perhaps it was during his tenure at the Artisan's Pavilion.
Whenever someone came seeking the vast troves of Gate archives, he'd instinctively call out—
"Brother Hong, where's this book?"
Only after a long silence would he remember: Hong had gone northward to study and never returned.
Left with no choice, he'd comb through the shelves volume by volume, emerging half a shichen later covered in dust with the requested text—only to find the lecture-bound colleagues long gone.

Or maybe it happened during his shifts at Yuling Hall.
Endless queues of patients with intricate mechanical ailments would overwhelm his senses.
How he wished Brother Tu were there—no obscure mechanism diagram could faze that walking encyclopedia.
But turning instinctively for help, he'd recall Tu too had returned home, leaving him to decipher blueprints alone.

Such scenes repeated endlessly that first year after both seniors departed.
Perhaps they recurred later too—only... gradually he forgot the self that always sought assistance.
As both mentors faded from his world, the once-protected junior finally stepped onto life's stage alone.
Fourteen winters after their leaving, Mount Jian bestowed a new name: Hu.
Like the yellow swan soaring a thousand miles.
Thus was Kuang Anshi renamed.

Rivers flow beyond the realm of earth, and mountain hues shimmer between presence and absence. Sun Yuan once gazed upon the Scenic Scroll of the Three Hundred Miles of Jialing River. Inspired, he climbed to a high peak. In a moment of exhilaration, he wielded his fan with the flourish of splattered ink, as if painting with the mountains themselves, each stroke unstoppable, like a living landscape. But once the trance faded, he could never use that fan technique again.
Ten years passed. A bell chimed in the clouds. And in that instant, Sun Yuan recalled the feeling, and the Inkwell Fan resurfaced in the jianghu once more.

Its full title is The Winning Endgame of White: Breaking the Chariot to Seize the River String, recorded in the Xiyuan Studio edition of Shilin Guangji, printed during the Zhishun reign of the Yuan dynasty. 
Shilin Guangji is the earliest known book to document Xiangqi (Chinese chess), compiled by Chen Yuanjing at the close of the Southern Song. Though the original Song edition is lost, surviving Yuan and Ming versions were later expanded and edited. The Xiyuan edition stands out for its early date and rich collection of recorded games, hence its value as a reference.
